Certificate inspector

Paste a certificate chain or probe a live TLS endpoint and find out whether the chain is complete, every link verifies, the hostname is covered and the private key matches.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsmonitoring.probe_free
📍 WhereTop bar → Tools (wrench) → Certificate inspector

What is it?#

The certificate inspector answers "will a client accept this certificate?". You either paste PEM text, or let SATOM open a TLS connection to a server and read what it presents. It puts the chain in leaf-first order, cryptographically checks each link, looks for the missing intermediate, and reports expiry, weak keys, hostname coverage and — if you supply it — whether a private key belongs to the certificate.

What does it do?#

  • Accepts a single certificate, a fullchain file, or a whole openssl s_client -showcerts transcript (annotation lines and CRLF endings are tolerated). Up to 12 certificates are read from one paste.
  • Orders the chain leaf → intermediate(s) → root, and lists certificates that belong to no position in the chain.
  • Verifies every link by checking the child's signature with the parent's public key — not by comparing names.
  • Decides whether the chain is complete: the top certificate is either a self-signed root in the bundle, or its issuer is found by name in the SATOM server's own CA trust store.
  • Checks a hostname against the SAN list (or the CN when there is no SAN) using the standard wildcard rule: a wildcard covers exactly one label and never the apex.
  • Compares a pasted private key with the leaf certificate.
  • Flags expiry, not-yet-valid, RSA keys below 2048 bits, MD5/SHA-1 signatures, self-signed leaves, out-of-order bundles and an included root.

Requirements#

  • For Paste PEM: nothing.
  • For Probe a host: the SATOM server must be able to reach the target on the network. To read the full chain from a live server, the openssl binary must be installed on the SATOM node; without it only the leaf certificate can be read and chain completeness is reported as UNKNOWN. The probe tab tells you which case applies before you click.

Permissions#

Action Needs
Open the inspector, paste PEM Any read permission (the coarse view key, granted for example by monitoring.view)
Probe an appliance from the Inventory destination list Any read permission (only appliances you can see in the current ADOM are listed)
Probe a free target (host:port or URL) <a class="dc-perm" href="permissions.html#monitoring-probe_free" title="Probe free targets — Point the certificate inspector and the transaction tracer at a
host SATOM does not manage. Inventory destinations never need this.">monitoring.probe_free — users with users.manage also qualify

Without monitoring.probe_free the free-target box is disabled and shows a permission required badge. A request that bypasses the box is refused with the message shown in Troubleshooting and the refusal is written to the audit log.

How to use#

Check a certificate file (Paste PEM)#

  1. Open Tools → Certificate inspector. The Paste PEM tab is selected.
  2. Paste the certificate or fullchain into Certificate / fullchain (PEM).
  3. Optional: type the name clients use into Hostname to check (for example shop.example.com).
  4. Optional: paste the matching key into Private key. It is checked in memory against the leaf and is never stored or logged.
  5. If the key is encrypted, type its passphrase into Key passphrase (a password field; like the key, it is used in memory only).
  6. Click Inspect.

Check a live server (Probe a host)#

  1. Open the Probe a host tab.
  2. Either pick an appliance from Inventory destination, or type a target in …or a free target — host, host:port, [IPv6]:port or a full https:// URL.
  3. Optional: type a name into SNI / hostname to check. SATOM sends it as SNI and checks the certificate against it; left empty, the target's own host is used.
  4. Click Probe. SATOM resolves the target once and connects to that address.

ℹ️Note

When you pick an inventory appliance, SATOM connects to the appliance's management address and port. Appliances are usually reached by IP address, so the hostname check will normally report Probed by address, so no name could match (informational). To check the name a real client uses, type that name in SNI / hostname to check, or probe the name as a free target.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: the Paste PEM tab has a Key passphrase field for encrypted keys and the Probe tab an optional SNI / hostname to check field; the inspector now needs a read permission instead of sign-in alone.

Read the result#

The result shows, from top to bottom:

  • A chain banner: Chain complete, Chain incomplete, or Chain completeness: UNKNOWN.
  • Findings, sorted critical → warning → info, each with a suggested fix.
  • One card per certificate (leaf, intermediate, root) with Subject, Issuer, Valid, Days left, Key, Signature hash, Serial, SHA-256 fingerprint and SAN.
  • Link verification: each child → parent link and whether the signature verified.
  • Hostname and Private key cards when you supplied them.
  • For a probe: the address that was actually dialled, the SNI, protocol and cipher.

Configuration#

Field Description Required Example
Certificate / fullchain (PEM) One or more BEGIN CERTIFICATE blocks, in any order Yes (paste) contents of fullchain.pem
Hostname to check Name to test against the SAN/CN list No shop.example.com
Private key PEM private key to compare with the leaf No contents of privkey.pem
Key passphrase Passphrase of an encrypted private key (up to 256 characters) Only for an encrypted key —
Inventory destination An appliance visible to you in the current ADOM One of the two (probe) fweb-01 — 192.0.2.10:443
…or a free target host, host:port, [v6]:port or http(s):// URL One of the two (probe) https://shop.example.com/
SNI / hostname to check Name sent as SNI and checked against the SAN/CN list; defaults to the target host No shop.example.com

Limits: pasted text is capped at 256 KB; only http:// and https:// URLs are accepted; the probe times out after 6 seconds.

Findings reference#

Severity Finding title (as shown) Meaning
Critical The chain is incomplete The issuer of the last presented certificate is neither in the bundle nor in this server's trust store. Clients fail with unable to get local issuer certificate.
Critical A chain link does not verify Two adjacent certificates are from different issuances.
Critical <name> has EXPIRED / expires in N days (≤ 7) / is not valid yet Validity problem.
Critical No presented name covers <host> The hostname is not in the SAN list.
Critical The private key does not match this certificate The key and certificate come from different issuances.
Critical A block is not a certificate A pasted block could not be parsed.
Warning <name> expires in N days (8–30) Schedule the renewal.
Warning <name> has a N-bit RSA key / is signed with md5 or sha1 Weak key or hash.
Warning The leaf is self-signed Expected on an appliance's factory GUI certificate, not on a published service.
Warning N certificate(s) belong to no position in this chain Extra, unrelated certificates in the bundle.
Warning The certificates are not in leaf-first order Some clients reject this order.
Info Chain completeness was not measured Only the leaf was read (no openssl on the node).
Info Probed by address, so no name could match Probe by IP; expected for a management GUI.
Info The root is included in the bundle Harmless, but unnecessary bytes on every handshake.
Info OpenSSL's own verdict openssl returned a non-zero verify code; shown as extra context.
Info A chain link could not be verified The signature algorithm is not supported by this build — neither confirmed nor denied.
Info The private key was not checked The key could not be parsed (for example, it is encrypted and no passphrase, or a wrong one, was given).

Example#

🧪Example — A wildcard that "works in testing"

You paste the fullchain for *.example.com and type example.com in Hostname to check. The verdict is critical: No presented name covers example.com — a wildcard covers one label (www.example.com) but not the apex. Reissue with example.com added to the SAN list.

Result#

  • Paste: nothing leaves the SATOM process and nothing is stored.
  • Probe: one outbound TLS connection from the SATOM server. Every probe is written to the audit log as cert_inspect.probe (target, mode, dialled address, SNI, error if any); every refused free-target attempt as cert_inspect.probe_denied. See Audit log.

Troubleshooting#

"No PEM certificate block found. Paste the text between -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----END CERTIFICATE----- (a fullchain may hold several)."#

Possible causes - You pasted a DER/binary file, a private key only, or a CSR.

Solution 1. Convert or export the certificate as PEM and paste it again.

Verification - The result shows at least one certificate card.

"Free-target probing requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission. Inventory destinations remain available."#

Possible causes - Your profile does not include monitoring.probe_free.

Solution 1. Pick the appliance from Inventory destination instead, or 2. Ask an administrator to add the permission to your profile.

Verification - The …or a free target box is enabled and has no permission required badge.

"Not an inventory destination."#

Possible causes - The selected appliance is no longer visible to you (deleted, moved to maintenance, or belongs to another ADOM).

Solution 1. Close and reopen the inspector to refresh the list.

"… is not in the inventory for this request. Switch the tool to free-target mode to dial a host SATOM does not manage."#

Possible causes - The host you selected does not match an appliance address in the current ADOM.

Solution 1. Use the free-target box (requires monitoring.probe_free).

"cloud instance-metadata address — it serves credentials to anything that can reach it, so SATOM never dials it"#

Possible causes - The target (or one of the addresses its name resolves to) is a cloud metadata address such as 169.254.169.254. This is refused in every mode and cannot be configured.

Solution 1. Probe the real service address instead.

"port N is not an HTTP/TLS port — dialling it from the server cannot produce a meaningful result"#

Possible causes - The port is one SATOM never dials: 0, 22, 25, 465, 587, 6379 or 11211.

Solution 1. Use the TLS port of the service.

"Could not read a certificate from host:port (address) — …"#

Possible causes - The server is unreachable from the SATOM node, the port is not TLS, or the connection timed out (timed out after 6s).

Solution 1. Confirm the service listens on that port and the SATOM node can reach it. 2. Try the Transaction tracer for TCP/TLS timing details.

The result says "Chain completeness: UNKNOWN."#

Possible causes - openssl is not installed on the SATOM node, so only the leaf certificate could be read. This is not the same as incomplete.

Solution 1. Install openssl on the node, or 2. Paste the server's fullchain file into the Paste PEM tab.

Verification - The probe tab note reads The full chain is read with openssl s_client, so chain completeness is measured.

"The private key was not checked — this private key is encrypted — supply its passphrase"#

Possible causes - The pasted key is passphrase-protected and Key passphrase was left empty.

Solution 1. Type the key's passphrase into Key passphrase and click Inspect again.

Verification - The Private key card shows whether the key matches the leaf. A wrong passphrase reports the private key could not be parsed instead.

Advanced#

Advanced How completeness is decided

The chain is assembled by name (subject → issuer). Each adjacent pair is then verified by signature. Above the last presented certificate, SATOM looks for the issuer's distinguished name in the server's CA bundle (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL, openSUSE or Alpine paths, falling back to certifi). That last step is a name match, not a signature check, and the banner says so.

Advanced Destination policy for probes

Names are resolved once; every returned address must pass the policy, and the connection is made to the resolved address (not re-resolved), with the hostname sent as SNI. Loopback, link-local and private (RFC 1918) addresses are allowed on purpose. Unspecified, multicast, reserved and cloud-metadata addresses are refused. URLs containing credentials (user@host) are refused.
